# Question 1: Treatment Effects Using the Lalonde Data

## Data and Objective

The `cps1re74.csv` dataset is available in this repository under the **Causal Inference** folder. The objective is to estimate the effect of treatment status (`treat`) on real earnings in 1978 (`re78`). Two additional indicator variables are generated to identify individuals whose earnings were zero in 1974 or 1975.

The simple regression model is

$$
\mathrm{re78}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{treat}_i + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $\beta_1$ represents the unadjusted difference in mean 1978 earnings between the treatment and comparison groups.

## Load and Prepare the Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

lalonde <- read.table(
  "C:/Users/USER/Downloads/cps1re74.csv",
  header = TRUE
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    u74 = as.numeric(re74 == 0),
    u75 = as.numeric(re75 == 0)
  )

dim(lalonde)
head(lalonde)
```

The variables `u74` and `u75` equal 1 when earnings in the corresponding year are zero and 0 otherwise.

## 1(a) Regression of `re78` on `treat`

Estimate the simple linear regression model:

$$
\mathrm{re78}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{treat}_i + \varepsilon_i.
$$

```{r}
m1 <- lm(re78 ~ treat, data = lalonde)
summary(m1)
```

The estimated coefficient of `treat` gives the estimated difference in mean 1978 earnings between treated and untreated individuals. Describe the coefficient, its statistical significance, and the model's $R^2$.

## 1(b) Regression of `re78` on All Available Predictors

Fit a multiple linear regression model including `treat` and all other available predictors, including the two generated indicators.

$$
\mathrm{re78}_i =
\beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{treat}_i
+ \sum_{j=2}^{p}\beta_j X_{ij} + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $X_{ij}$ denotes the additional predictors.

```{r}
m2 <- lm(re78 ~ ., data = lalonde)
summary(m2)
```

In this model, the coefficient of `treat` estimates the difference in 1978 earnings between treatment groups after adjusting for the other included predictors.

## 1(c) Regression Models Using All Subsets of Predictors

Fit every possible subset of the ten candidate predictors while including `treat` in every model.

The candidate predictors are:

```{r}
x <- c(
  "age", "educ", "black", "hispan", "married", "nodegree",
  "re74", "re75", "u74", "u75"
)
```

For each subset $S$, the regression model is

$$
\mathrm{re78}_i =
\beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{treat}_i
+ \sum_{j \in S}\beta_j X_{ij} + \varepsilon_i.
$$

### Fit All Subset Models

```{r}
y <- "re78"

combs <- unlist(
  lapply(
    0:length(x),
    function(k) combn(x, k, simplify = FALSE)
  ),
  recursive = FALSE
)

res <- data.frame(
  regs = character(),
  coef = numeric(),
  p_value = numeric(),
  direction = character(),
  significance = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (j in combs) {

  rhs <- c("treat", j)

  formula <- as.formula(
    paste(y, "~", paste(rhs, collapse = " + "))
  )

  fit <- lm(formula, data = lalonde)
  coef_table <- summary(fit)$coefficients

  treatment_estimate <- coef_table["treat", "Estimate"]
  treatment_p_value <- coef_table["treat", "Pr(>|t|)"]

  res <- rbind(
    res,
    data.frame(
      regs = if (length(j) == 0) {
        "(No additional predictors)"
      } else {
        paste(j, collapse = ", ")
      },
      coef = treatment_estimate,
      p_value = treatment_p_value,
      direction = ifelse(
        treatment_estimate > 0,
        "Positive",
        "Negative"
      ),
      significance = ifelse(
        treatment_p_value < 0.05,
        "Significant",
        "Not significant"
      ),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

head(res)
```

There are $2^{10}=1024$ possible subsets of the ten candidate predictors. Thus, 1,024 regression models are fitted, each including `treat`.

### Count Significant and Nonsignificant Coefficients

```{r}
table(
  factor(
    res$significance,
    levels = c("Significant", "Not significant")
  )
)
```

### Count Positive and Negative Significant Coefficients

```{r}
significant_direction_counts <- table(
  factor(
    res$direction,
    levels = c("Positive", "Negative")
  ),
  factor(
    res$significance,
    levels = c("Significant", "Not significant")
  )
)

significant_direction_counts

# Positively significant coefficients
significant_direction_counts["Positive", "Significant"]

# Negatively significant coefficients
significant_direction_counts["Negative", "Significant"]

# Nonsignificant coefficients
sum(res$significance == "Not significant")
```

### Visualize Statistical Significance

```{r}
ggplot(res, aes(x = significance)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Significance of Treatment Coefficients",
    x = "Statistical significance",
    y = "Number of regression models"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Distribution of Treatment Coefficients

```{r}
ggplot(res, aes(x = coef)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Treatment Coefficients Across All Subset Models",
    x = "Estimated coefficient of treat",
    y = "Number of models"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Models with the Smallest P-values

```{r}
res |>
  arrange(p_value) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

# Question 2: Race and Callback Rates in the Resume Data

## Data and Objective

The `resume.csv` dataset is provided through Google Classroom. The objective is to examine whether race is associated with callback status. The variable `race` identifies the race group, while `call` indicates whether an applicant received a callback.

## Load the Data

```{r}
resume <- read_csv("C:/Users/USER/Downloads/resume.csv")

head(resume)
glimpse(resume)
```

## 2(a) Summary Table by Race

Calculate the total number of applicants, numbers of male and female applicants, number of callbacks, and callback rate for each race group.

```{r}
race_summary <- resume |>
  group_by(race) |>
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    male = sum(sex == "male"),
    female = sum(sex == "female"),
    callback = sum(call == 1),
    callback_rate = mean(call),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

race_summary
```

The callback rate is calculated as

$$
\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{callback}}
=
\frac{\text{Number of applicants receiving callbacks}}
{\text{Total number of applicants}}.
$$

## 2(b) Contingency Table and Chi-squared Test

Construct a contingency table of race and callback status.

```{r}
tab <- table(resume$race, resume$call)

tab
```

The hypotheses are

$$
H_0: \text{Race and callback status are independent},
$$

$$
H_1: \text{Race and callback status are associated}.
$$

The Pearson chi-squared test statistic is

$$
\chi^2 =
\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c}
\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}},
$$

where $O_{ij}$ and $E_{ij}$ are the observed and expected cell counts.

```{r}
chisq.test(tab)
```

At the 5% significance level, compare the p-value with 0.05 to determine whether there is evidence of an association between race and callback status.

## 2(c) Subgroup Analyses by Sex

Repeat the contingency-table analysis separately for male and female applicants.

### Male Applicants

```{r}
male_data <- resume |>
  filter(sex == "male")

tab_m <- table(male_data$race, male_data$call)

tab_m
chisq.test(tab_m)
```

### Female Applicants

```{r}
female_data <- resume |>
  filter(sex == "female")

tab_f <- table(female_data$race, female_data$call)

tab_f
chisq.test(tab_f)
```

Compare the p-values and callback patterns from the two subgroup analyses. Discuss whether the evidence of an association between race and callback status appears similar for male and female applicants.
